# Introduction 
exploreSE is a package that provides an interactive Shiny-based user interface for exploring transcriptional data and analysis results stored in [SummarizedExperiment](https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/SummarizedExperiment.html) or [DeeDeeExperiment](https://bioconductor.org/packages//release/bioc/html/DeeDeeExperiment.html) format. The aim is to facilitate easy comparison between different model approaches on a single data set. 

The package can be installed via the `BiocManager` by starting R and running: 
```{r install, eval = FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("BiocManager")
}

BiocManager::install("exploreSE")
```

Once installed, the package can be loaded with the following bit of code:

```{r library}
library(exploreSE)
```

To explore the results of differential expression analysis, we need to organise them in a specific structure, and you will learn how to do that in this vignette. If you want to explore on your own, you can run the following code and start exploring the example data.

```{r quickstart, eval=FALSE}
example(exploreSE, ask = FALSE)
```



# Setting up the data
For the purposes of this example, we'll be using the `airway` data. It is part of the [airway](https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/data/experiment/html/airway.html) package, containing RNA-Seq data from different airway smooth muscle cell lines either untreated or treated with dexamethasone.

```{r airway-dataset, message=FALSE}
library(airway)
data(airway)
airway
```

Out of the box, the `airway` object is a `SummarizedExperiment` object, containing eight samples from four cell lines. This information is available in `colData(airway)`.

```{r coldata_example}
colData(airway)
```

In this vignette, we will subset `airway` to only contain protein-coding genes. The required information is stored in its `rowData`, accessible through `rowData(airway)`.

```{r rowdata_example}
rowData(airway)
```

```{r example_filtering}
dim(airway)
airway <- airway[rowData(airway)$gene_biotype == "protein_coding", ]
dim(airway)
```

Let's start our analysis. Using the [DESeq2](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/DESeq2.html) package, we will convert `airway` into a `DESeqDataSet` and build a simple model based on the dexamethasone stimulation stored in the `dex` variable. 


```{r example_adding_baseline}
library(DESeq2)
airway <- DESeqDataSet(airway, design = ~dex)
airway <- DESeq(airway)
baseline <- results(airway)
```

In addition, we'll build a second model, where we control for the effect of the cell line, stored in the `cell` variable: 

```{r example_adding_controlled}
design(airway) <- ~ cell + dex
airway <- DESeq(airway)
cell_controlled <- results(airway)
```

Using the [DeeDeeExperiment](https://bioconductor.org/packages//release/bioc/html/DeeDeeExperiment.html) package, we will store these results in their respective slots. 

```{r example_deedee}
library(DeeDeeExperiment)
airway <- DeeDeeExperiment(airway)
airway <- addDEA(airway, baseline)
airway <- addDEA(airway, cell_controlled)
```

Let's take a look:

```{r example_structure_showcase}
airway
```

In addition to differential expression analysis, we can also explore functional enrichment results, in this case a GO over-representation analysis (ORA). Here we use the `get.gos()` function from the `exploreSE` package, but it just populates the FEA slot of the DeeDeeExperiment. 


```{r example_gos, warning = FALSE}
airway <- get.gos(obj = airway, NAME = "baseline", gene_type = "ENSEMBL")
airway <- get.gos(obj = airway, NAME = "cell_controlled", gene_type = "ENSEMBL")
```

```{r example_showcase_with_gos}
airway
```

Now that our data is ready, we can start exploring. 

# Launching the App
The simplest way to launch the app is through a call to the `exploreSE()` function. Without any arguments, the app opens and you can load in any .RDS file. Alternatively, you can supply the `file` argument, defining the path to the file, or the `object` argument when you have the object already loaded.

```{r running_the_app, eval=FALSE}
app <- exploreSE(object = airway)
shiny::runApp(app, port = 1234)
```

## About

![About.](screenshots/about.png)

After starting the app, you are presented with an "About" page. You can navigate to different tabs by clicking on the thumbnails or learn more about the possibilities of the app through the question marks. 


There are 9 tabs to choose from inside the app: 

1. About: a quick introduction to the app (you are here).
2. Data Overview: an overview of the metadata of your samples
3. PCA: a principal component analysis of the samples
4. Gene Expression: the expression of a selected gene is visualised
5. DE Results: the currently selected DE comparison is summarised and visualised
6. Volcano Plot: a volcano plot of the selected DE comparison
7. Enrichment Results: the available enrichment results are plotted
8. FC FC: the fold changes of two DE comparisons are compared
9. Context: your own gene lists are overlaid on the selected DE comparison



## Overview 

Initially, you can navigate to the "Data Overview" tab, where you will find an overview of the metadata in the `colData` of the relevant `SummarizedExperiment`, as well as a searchable and scrollable view of the same table. 
On the left-hand side, you can load in a different object from the local environment if desired under the "Data Input" header - should you start up the app without any data, the "Use Demo Data" checkbox will be checked and some demo data will be generated for you. 
Below that, you will find some options for your data exploration throughout the app. Options that are specific to one panel are integrated into that panel, but globally relevant options appear in the sidebar as needed.
You will have your choice of the relevant gene identifier; by default it picks the `gene_name` column of your `rowData` if present, and otherwise the first suitable column, but this can be changed with the drop-down menu.
Secondly, you can pick your differential expression analysis; these come from the relevant slots from the underlying `DeeDeeExperiment` or `metadata()`.
Finally, the adjusted p-value and log2 fold change cutoffs that define differentially expressed genes (default: 0.05 and 1) are set in the sidebar as well. They apply to all tabs that use them: Gene Expression, DE Results, Volcano Plot, FC FC and Context. 




## PCA view
Progressing through the app, you can navigate to the PCA tab.
![View of the PCA tab](screenshots/pca_baseline.png)

You can select the colouring scheme of the points in the drop-down menu, as well as how many genes are used to calculate the PCA. 
In the `airway` data set, the dexamethasone treatment, saved in the `dex` variable, is the primary variable of interest, but you can also select others from the drop-down menu. 

![Alternative colouring of the PCA](screenshots/pca_dex.png)


## Expression plotting

Navigating to the Gene Expression tab, you can check the expression of selected genes. By selecting a value in the Color/Group by drop-down menu, you can select the value on the x-axis. You can also include/exclude certain levels of that variable through the tick boxes on the left. The gene being plotted is selected by the "Select Gene" drop-down menu, which is searchable. Any values visible in the plot can be exported from the table below. 

![Overview of the Gene Expression panel](screenshots/expression.png)


## DE Results

The heart of this application is the comparison of different possible models and within this tab, we are starting that process. 

![Differential expression overview for the baseline model.](screenshots/de_baseline.png)

On the top of the page, a little overview indicates all the comparisons found in the respective slots. 
Below, a bar chart indicates the number of differentially expressed genes. The specifics of the results can be looked up in a table below and exported. 

This view also exists for each comparison; selecting a different comparison from the drop-down menu on the left-hand side refreshes the view:

![Differential expression overview for the cell-controlled model.](screenshots/de_controlled.png)

## Volcano plot

A graphical overview of the differential expression can be found in the Volcano Plot tab.

![Volcano plot of the baseline model.](screenshots/volcano_baseline.png)

The cutoffs for significance are taken from the sidebar, where the colour code can be changed as well. On the top of this tab, you can choose whether and how many of the top genes are labelled, and highlight genes of your choice. Again, this view depends on the selected comparison. 

## Enrichment results 

For interpretation of these results, you often rely on the different enrichment methods to determine which biological themes or pathways are altered in a given comparison. These results are visualised in the Enrichment Results tab.

![Enrichment results for the baseline model.](screenshots/gos_baseline.png)

In this case, we are looking at the GO term enrichments for the baseline model. Like before, some graphical adjustments can be set at the top. Below, we have two bar charts, one for each direction of the comparison. The genes driving the enrichment can be shown inside the bars and upon hover after ticking the box in the options. 

## Comparison of Fold Changes

Direct comparison of fold changes across models can generate insights into the differences. For this, two models can be selected and their respective fold changes plotted against each other.

![FC-FC plot of the baseline and cell-controlled models.](screenshots/fc_fc.png)


Below the plot, a table highlights genes with a fold change difference larger than the selected threshold (default: 1). This table can be downloaded.


## Putting your DE results into context

One way to interpret your results is to put them into a larger context. Looking for enriched biological themes, as above, is one way to do this, but the context can also be more specific. In the Context tab of `exploreSE`, you can add your own gene lists, for example known genetic risk factors for the disease in question or genes of interest from other experiments. To add a gene list, click the "Add context" button and either paste the gene identifiers directly or upload a delimited file with one gene list per column and the name of each context as its column header. The gene identifiers are matched against all gene identifier columns of the `rowData`, so a list can use any of them, or even a mix, and is shown in the identifier selected in the sidebar. Matching is case-sensitive, and entries that are not found are listed under "Get the Overlap".

Context lists can also be passed when launching the app, as a named list of gene vectors through the `context` argument of `exploreSE()`. The names of the list are used as the context names. `exploreSE` comes with example contexts in `example_contexts`: a set of well-known glucocorticoid response genes (`dex_response`) and genetic risk factors for several cardiovascular diseases, such as aortic valve stenosis, aortic aneurysms and coronary artery disease (see `?example_contexts` for the full list and sources). All are gene symbols that match the `gene_name` column of the `rowData`. Here, we pass the glucocorticoid response genes:

```{r context_argument, eval=FALSE}
data("example_contexts", package = "exploreSE")
app <- exploreSE(
  object = airway,
  context = example_contexts["dex_response"]
)
shiny::runApp(app, port = 1234)
```

The same contexts are also available as a file with one context per column, which you can use to try the "Add context" upload:

```{r context_file, eval=FALSE}
system.file("extdata", "example_contexts.csv", package = "exploreSE")
```

The context is then overlaid on the volcano plot of the selected comparison, and its overrepresentation among both up- and downregulated genes is tested with a hypergeometric test, using all tested genes as the background.

![A dexamethasone response signature overlaid on the differential expression results.](screenshots/context.png)

An important methodological note: the results of this overrepresentation analysis should be taken with a grain of salt, since a) the p-values are not adjusted for multiple testing and b) the (researcher-selected) context is probably not independent of the experiment whose results are being analysed. For example, the response signature shown here is partly derived from the `airway` data set itself, so its enrichment is circular.

# FAQ

**Q: How do I add results into the SummarizedExperiment?**
A: The easiest way is to use the `DeeDeeExperiment` extension of the `SummarizedExperiment` class. You can use the dedicated DEA and FEA slots. There is a detailed explanation [here](https://bioconductor.org/packages//release/bioc/vignettes/DeeDeeExperiment/inst/doc/DeeDeeExperiment_manual.html). If you do not want that, you can add them to the `SummarizedExperiment` metadata, using `de_results` and `fe_results` as names. 

**Q: Can I use the explorer to perform analysis?**
A: No, this app is only designed to visualise already performed analyses. All decisions on what to test and which enrichments to run should happen before you start the app and make use of the package.
